blocks.p: In two dimensions, two lines either meet or are parallel. In three dimensions there is a third case: **skew lines**, which are not parallel and never meet because they don't lie in a common plane. Which formula you use depends on which case you have.

table.caption: Which formula to use
rows: Not parallel, and that product is not 0
$\vec{b_1}$ and $\vec{b_2}$ are multiples of each other

blocks.p: For two lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a_1}+\lambda\vec{b_1}$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{a_2}+\mu\vec{b_2}$ that don't intersect, the shortest distance between them is:

**Why it works:** $\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2}$ is perpendicular to both lines, so the shortest connecting segment runs along it. Dividing by its length gives a unit vector in that direction, and the dot product projects the gap between the two starting points $\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1}$ onto it.
Find the shortest distance between $\vec{r}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\lambda(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}+\mu(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$.
Find the shortest distance between $\vec{r}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$.
The dot product came out negative, which only means the cross product points the other way. The absolute value in the formula takes care of it.

**Solution:** Both lines have direction $\vec{b} = (2,3,6)$, so they are parallel and $\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2} = \vec{0}$: the skew-line formula would divide by zero. Use the parallel-line formula with $\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1} = (2,1,-1)$:

For $\dfrac{x-x_1}{a_1}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b_1}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c_1}$ and $\dfrac{x-x_2}{a_2}=\dfrac{y-y_2}{b_2}=\dfrac{z-z_2}{c_2}$, read off $\vec{a_1} = (x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $\vec{b_1} = (a_1, b_1, c_1)$, and the same for the second line. The numerator of the skew-line formula is then a single determinant:

blocks.math: \begin{vmatrix} x_2-x_1 & y_2-y_1 & z_2-z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix}

blocks.p: If that determinant is 0 and the lines aren't parallel, they intersect.

list: **Using the skew formula on parallel lines.** If $\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2} = \vec{0}$, switch to the parallel-line formula instead of reporting an undefined answer.
**Reading the point and direction the wrong way round.** In $\dfrac{x+1}{2}$, the point has $x_1 = -1$ (the sign flips) and the direction ratio is 2.
**Dropping the absolute value.** A distance can't be negative. A negative dot product just means the cross product happened to point the other way.
**Forgetting to check for intersection.** A numerator of 0 means the lines meet, so the distance is 0, not "no answer".
